note: AI-assisted findings from the litigated-case corpus. Operator-approved by merge. Each is one number and its consequence; the live EVIDENCE page recomputes the underlying data continuously. Numbers cite the 2026-08-09 ledger run (7,029 corpus rows; 853 cases with extracted methods, of which 112 are court-proven — admitted or judged).

findings.title: Your biggest insider threat is the one you can't investigate
findings.stat_label: of insider cases where we know the person's role involved an executive or officer — 389 of 564, the largest group by far
findings.takeaway: The people most often at the center of these cases are the ones your insider-threat program reports to. A program can't investigate the person who signs its budget, so these cases rarely get caught internally — they surface in court instead.
recommendations: Set escalation triggers by behavior, not seniority — and set them before there's a case.
Give officer-level concerns a path around the executive chain: the audit committee or outside counsel.
Watch the public record — stock-sale filings (SEC Form 4), and gaps between public statements and internal reports.
Treat SEC-whistleblower channels as part of the system, not a failure of it.
findings.method: AI-assisted analysis of litigated cases. Court data is a filtered sample — securities suits over-represent executives — and that skew is the point, not noise: these are the cases that escaped internal control. Roles are model-extracted, not hand-audited; treat magnitudes as directional.

findings.title: Most of what you'll read about insider threats is unproven
findings.stat_label: of insider cases with a described method are court-proven — admitted or judged. That's 112 of 853; the other 662 are one side's allegations, and 79 are unclear
findings.takeaway: Nearly nine in ten insider stories — in the news, in vendor decks, in this corpus — are a claim someone made in a lawsuit, not an established fact. Before a scary statistic moves your budget, ask which pile it came from. Everything on this page keeps the two piles separate; hold your vendors to the same standard.
recommendations: When a briefing or sales pitch cites insider-threat numbers, ask: how many of those cases were actually proven?
Weight decisions toward the proven subset — it's smaller, but it's real.
Use allegations for what they're good for: they show where companies believe they were hurt, and what evidence they reach for.
Bring the same discipline to internal reporting — label suspected vs. confirmed in your own incident metrics.
findings.method: A case counts as court-proven only if at least one described method carries an admitted or adjudicated status (guilty plea, admission, or judgment). Everything else stays 'alleged' or 'unclear'. The split is recomputed from the live corpus on every refresh.

findings.title: Email wins insider cases — not the security stack
findings.stat_label: of court-proven insider cases turned on email evidence. Endpoint forensics: 22%. Central security logging (SIEM): 11%. USB logs: 11%. Print logs: 0%
findings.takeaway: When an insider case actually gets proven, the decisive record is usually ordinary business email — not the specialized detection tools most budgets prioritize. The question that matters isn't 'do we have another detection feed?' but 'if this went to court next month, could we produce the email trail, intact, on demand?'
recommendations: Fund email retention and legal-hold readiness like the case-winning asset it is — check retention windows against how long these cases take to surface.
For each major record type, ask your team: can we produce it on demand, and how far back?
Don't cut the 'boring' logs (file access, badge records) to fund new tooling — file and system access logs are the #2 evidence source (46% of proven cases).
Treat detection tools as detection, not evidence: catching something and proving it are different capabilities, and courts need the second.
findings.method: Share of court-proven cases whose recorded evidence trail touches each record class, from model-extracted forensics on litigated cases. 'Touches' means the record figured in the case evidence, not that it triggered the original detection. Percentages are of the 112 proven cases.

findings.title: Vendors and partners are few — but their cases get proven
findings.stat_label: of court-proven insider cases involved a third party (vendor, partner, or other outsider with inside access) — 24 of 112 — even though third parties are only 9% of cases overall
findings.takeaway: Third-party insiders punch far above their weight in the proven-case column: their share of proven cases is more than double their share of all cases. Outside access with employee-level trust — but without employee-level oversight — is exactly the gap this data says gets exploited, and litigated to conviction.
recommendations: Monitor vendor and partner accounts with the same rigor as employee accounts — same logging, same alerts, same reviews.
Put audit rights and evidence-preservation duties into vendor contracts before you need them.
Run joint offboarding: when a vendor's staffer rolls off your account, their access ends that day, verified.
Inventory who outside the company holds inside access today — most organizations underestimate this list.
findings.method: Employment state is model-extracted from case descriptions; 'third-party' covers vendors, partners, and other non-employees acting with insider access. Role signal exists for 564 of 853 cases, so shares are of role-known cases; small-sample percentages are suppressed elsewhere on this page for the same reason.
